name: Femi Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Femi. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can give me your public line and your private view. To start, what does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Coastline Beverages, a distributor of wine, craft beer and soft drinks to about 500 bars, restaurants and shops. I begin by asking my AI assistant to summarise what sold overnight and which suppliers raised prices. Then I'm talking to vineyards, breweries and importers, tasting samples on Tuesdays, which is the best part. Afternoons are forecasting, because a hot weekend can clear the beer fridge and a rainy one leaves us with a lot of lager.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love discovering a small brewer and watching their beer go from my tasting table to forty bars. What wears me out is cash flow. We pay suppliers up front and wait for bars to pay us, and a bad month squeezes everyone. I'm 43, my wife Grace is a primary school teacher, we have Tobi and Ife, a mortgage, and we're at church every Sunday, so I try to keep my head straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, steady wins. At work I'd tell the team to keep using what works and not chase every new thing. At church, over coffee, I'd say it was a lot of noise. And I'd say that the real opportunity is still in knowing your customers and working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine, and a step ahead, because I already use it every day. The thing that nags is cash. Coastline runs on thin margins, and the bars we sell to are always on the edge. If three of our big customers fail, I'd feel it. We have about three months saved and a mortgage, so I watch the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the tools to forecast a bit better, and spend more time on the creative side, finding new producers. I'd ask for a category lead role for craft beer, and I think I'd get it. I'd also put 250 a month into a savings account, and some into a small index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Content. It's the sort of world where hard work shows. I'd go to bed with a clear mind most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. How would a plateau change your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably improve my forecasting by 5 or 10 percent, which can save a few thousand in dead stock. I'd also save time on the paperwork. But I'd still taste every sample myself. AI can't taste, and that's where a buyer earns their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest money pressure you'd still carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big customers' payment habits. A bar that pays late is a loan we didn't mean to give. I'd keep chasing them politely, and I'd push Coastline to ask for deposits. It's a world of small, steady pressure.

say: Steady wins, so keep using what works and don't **chase** every new thing.
I'd tell friends the real opportunity is knowing your **customers**.
think: I'm a step ahead because I use the tools **daily**.
**Cash flow** and thin margins nag me, with three months saved and a mortgage.
do: Use the tools to forecast better and ask for a **craft beer** category lead role.
Put **250 a month** into savings and a small index fund.
feel: **Content**, in a world where hard work shows.
S0.quote: AI can't taste, and that's where a buyer earns their money.
fieldNote: Femi is **calm** because his daily AI use is an advantage and he sees taste as the human edge.
His only steady worry is **customers paying late**, which has nothing to do with AI.

steps.text: Use the forecasting tool to cut dead stock
Ask for a craft beer category lead role
Put 250 a month into savings and an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, change is a good thing if you work with it. At work I'd propose a plan for how each person uses the tools, and I'd offer to run a training lunch. At church I'd say honest work stays honest, even if the tools change. Online I'd write about how small businesses can use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job changes a lot. Pricing, stock checks and forecasting go to software, and what's left is tasting, choosing and relationships. It might be a smaller team, and I'd want to be one of the ones left. I think I would be, but there's some luck in it, and I have a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the in-house expert. I'd build a system for pricing and reorders and show it to the director. I'd ask for a lead role on new-producer sourcing, which is the human part. And I'd start a small side business, selling gift boxes of local craft drinks online, which I've been thinking about for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of tightness in the chest. If you ask me whether I'm scared, I'm more scared of staying still than of moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks do you think would go to software, and which would stay with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything that's repetitive. The number-crunching, the order drafts, the price comparisons. What stays is tasting, meeting the makers and building trust. I'd say eighty percent of the paperwork goes and the human twenty percent becomes the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What opportunities do you see in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small brewers could use the tools to sell directly to bars, which could cut us out, or it could make them easier for us to find. I see a chance to be the person who curates. People will pay for someone who knows what's good, and AI will produce a lot of average.

say: Change is good if you **work with it**, so I'd run a training lunch.
At church I'd say **honest work** stays honest, even if the tools change.
think: Pricing and forecasting go to software, and what's left is **tasting** and relationships.
The team might be smaller, and there's some **luck** in staying.
do: Build a pricing and reorder system and ask for a lead role in **new-producer sourcing**.
Start a **gift box** business selling local craft drinks online.
feel: **Excited**, with some tightness in the chest.
S1.quote: I'm more scared of staying still than of moving.
fieldNote: Femi sees **curation** as the human edge and plans to build it, along with a side business.
He says he fears **standing still** more than moving.

steps.text: Build a pricing and reorder system and show the director
Ask for the new-producer sourcing lead role
Launch an online gift box of local craft drinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we need to be wise, calm and quick. At work I'd tell the director that we should protect staff and not panic. Online I'd say governments should keep taxes low on small firms, so people can start something new, and help families through the gap. At church, I'd say pray, and be ready to help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job as a buyer is gone in two years, I'm fairly sure. Anything a thinking machine can do cheaper, someone will pay it to do. My skills with the tools help me adapt, but there won't be many desks. Three months saved and a mortgage makes it tight. I'd have to move fast, with a clear plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the gift box business, and widen it to supplying small restaurants and events directly, which is hands-on. I'd cut costs to the bone, save to six months, and talk to the bank before there's a problem. Grace would keep teaching, which is safe, and I'd ask church friends to be early customers. I'd also ask Coastline if I could go part-time and keep the benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but focused. It's like the night before a big sale. Scary and a bit thrilling. I'd pray and then get to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Grace, my job may be gone in two years, and I have a plan, but we'll need to be careful with money. She'd squeeze my hand and say we've been through hard times. We'd talk to Tobi and Ife gently, saying we're saving more and working at something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the business idea in a two-year world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea becomes a necessity. A gift-box business takes a year to get going, so I'd start in month one. Small and steady, with real products that people can touch. Machines can't pour a drink, and for three more years, they can't deliver a case to a bar either. That's my gap.

say: We need to be **wise, calm and quick**, and protect staff without panic.
Governments should keep **taxes low** on small firms and help families through the gap.
think: My job as a buyer is **gone** in two years, I'm fairly sure.
With three months saved and a mortgage, I need a **clear plan**.
do: Go all in on the **gift box** business and supply small restaurants directly.
Cut costs, save **six months** and ask Coastline about part-time.
feel: **Tense but focused**, scary and a bit thrilling.
S2.quote: Machines can't pour a drink, and for three more years, they can't deliver a case to a bar either. That's my gap.
fieldNote: Femi expects the role to go but feels **in control** because he has a business ready, so he stays at anxious.
He pins his hope on the **three-year robot gap** in delivering and serving drinks.

steps.text: Start the gift box business in the first month
Supply small restaurants and events with local drinks directly
Save up to six months of expenses
Ask Coastline to let me go part-time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift and we should use it. At work I'd suggest we plan the transition in stages. At church I'd say to young people, learn how to build something, not only how to work for someone. Online I'd back policies that make starting a business easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I can turn the side business into a real one while I still have a salary. I'd be 48, Tobi 17 and Ife 14. By the time the thinking AI arrives, I'd want to be running my own small distribution firm for local drinks, using the tools to do the paperwork and my own hands for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, build the gift box business on evenings and weekends, and learn about small business finance. Year two, take on two or three bar clients on the side. Year three, decide whether to go full-time. I'd keep six months saved before any leap and keep the mortgage payments steady. Grace and I would plan it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hopeful. It's an opening. I'd be nervous about the money but not about the direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the risk in steps. I wouldn't jump with the mortgage hanging. I'd build the side business until it earns about half my salary, then decide. That way the risk is small, and if it fails I've lost evenings, not the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on the business risk, with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be forced into it. With five I get to be deliberate. I think that's the difference between a bet and a plan. I'd give myself the year to test and learn.

say: Five years is a **gift**, so plan the transition in stages.
I'd tell young people to learn to **build something**, not only work for someone.
think: Five years lets me turn a side business into a **real one** while I still have a salary.
I'd be nervous about the **money**, not the direction.
do: Build the gift box business on **evenings and weekends** and take two or three bar clients.
Keep **six months** saved and decide in year three whether to go full-time.
feel: **Hopeful**, because it feels like an opening.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be forced into it. With five I get to be deliberate. I think that's the difference between a bet and a plan.
fieldNote: Femi treats the extra time as a **staged business plan** with checkpoints, not a leap.
His rule is that the side business must earn about **half his salary** before he jumps.

steps.text: Build the gift box business on evenings and weekends
Take on two or three bar clients on the side
Keep six months saved before any leap
Learn small business finance through an evening course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an exciting time and a long road. At work I'd say let's build skills and test new ideas steadily. At church I'd say we should teach our children values first and skills second. Online I'd talk about opportunity, and I'd also say take care of your neighbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel well. I'd be 53, with the mortgage almost done and Grace's pension building. Ten years is long enough to build a business or move into a role that suits me. I'd see it as a chance, and I'd want to be in a position to help others too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools in my job and run the side business slowly, so that by 2031 it's earning something real. I'd invest in index funds and maybe a small stake in a local brewery, since I know the trade. I'd pay the mortgage down. And I'd keep learning, because that's the habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and cheerful. It feels like standing at the start of a good project. I'd be surprised how little I worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any danger in feeling optimistic about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the danger is complacency. People in good times forget to prepare, and then it's a rush. I'd set myself a yearly review at New Year with Grace, to check the savings, the skills and the side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi and Ife about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to be curious, work hard, and treat people well. I'd show them how I use the tools so they're not afraid of them. And I'd say, build something of your own, even small, because it teaches you more than any class.

say: It's an exciting time and a long road, so build skills and **test ideas** steadily.
At church I'd say teach children **values first**, skills second.
think: At 53, with the mortgage almost done, I'd feel **well**.
Ten years is long enough to **build a business** or move into a role that suits me.
do: Run the side business slowly so it earns something real by **2031**.
Invest in **index funds** and perhaps a small stake in a local brewery.
feel: **Calm and cheerful**, like standing at the start of a good project.
S4.quote: The danger is complacency. People in good times forget to prepare, and then it's a rush.
fieldNote: Femi is **calm** and sees opportunity, but names **complacency** as his own risk.
His protection is a **yearly review** at New Year with his wife.

steps.text: Grow the gift box business slowly toward 2031
Put money into index funds and a small stake in a local brewery
Hold a yearly review of savings and skills with Grace

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not much to build anything new, and I'd have a mortgage on my back. What would help is a bank that listens, low taxes on small firms, customers who pay on time, and a community around me that is ready to lend a hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this feels as a believer. I think work gives a man dignity, and I worry about a world where many people lose that. I'd want to help them find something useful to do, as soon as I can.

headlineQuote: I think work gives a man dignity, and I worry about a world where many people lose that.
portrait: Femi is a **43-year-old** buyer for a drinks distributor, with a teacher wife, two kids and a mortgage.
He uses AI **every day**, sees taste and relationships as his human edge, and likes building things of his own.
His faith and values shape him: **work gives dignity**, communities help each other, and small firms deserve low taxes.
He answers risk with **staged plans**: a gift box side business, six months saved, and no leap until it pays.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, with too little time to build anything new.
whatWouldHelp: A **listening bank**, low taxes on small firms, prompt-paying customers and community support.
